parts.text:
The first three terms in ascending powers of $x$ in the binomial expansion of $(1+px)^{12}$ are given by
$1+18x+qx^2$
where $p$ and $q$ are constants.
Find the value of $p$ and the value of $q$.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
$1+\binom{12}{1}\times px+\binom{12}{2}\times(px)^2$ or $1+12px+\frac{12.11}{2}(px)^2$ M1: Correct structure for at least 1 of the underlined terms, including coefficients. Could be implied by e.g. 12p=18
$=(1+12px+66p^2x^2)$
$12p=18\Rightarrow p=$ M1: Compare coefficients of x and solve for p
$p=\frac{18}{12}\left(=\frac{3}{2}\right)$ A1: Correct value for p
$q=66\times\left(\text{their}\frac{3}{2}\right)^2$ M1: Substitutes their value of p into their coefficient of x^2 to find q
$q=148.5$ or equivalent A1: cao
Note: failing to square p in the x^2 term could score M1M1A1M1A0 (4/5) (gives q=99)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Given that when $\mathrm{f}(x)$ is divided by $(x-2)$ the remainder is 25,
(a) show that $2a+b=5$
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
$\mathrm{f}(2)=2(2)^3+(2)^2+2a+b=25$ M1: f($\pm2$)=25
$16+4+2a+b=25\Rightarrow2a+b=5$* A1: Correct completion to printed answer. If f(2) is not seen explicitly and "16+4+2a+b=25" is incorrect, score M0
Alternative by long division: $2x^3+x^2+ax+b\div(x-2)$, Quotient=$2x^2+5x+a+10$, Remainder=$2a+b+20$ M1: Attempt Quotient & Remainder: Needs a quotient of the form $2x^2+kx+f(a)$ and a remainder that is a function of a and b
$2a+b+20=25\Rightarrow2a+b=5$* A1: Correct completion to printed answer

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Given also that $(x+3)$ is a factor of $\mathrm{f}(x)$,
(b) find the value of $a$ and the value of $b$.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
$\mathrm{f}(-3)=2(-3)^3+(-3)^2-3a+b=0$ M1: f($\pm3$)=0
$2a+b=5$, $b-3a=45\to a=$ or $b=$ M1: Solves simultaneously to a= or b=
$a=-8$, $b=21$ A1,A1: First A1: One correct constant; Second A1: Both constants correct

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Use calculus to find the coordinates of the stationary point of $C$.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:

$x-9=0\Rightarrow x=9$ only A1: cso

questions.stem:
The first term of a geometric series is 5 and the common ratio is 1.2
For this series find, to 1 decimal place,

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) (i) the 20th term,
(ii) the sum of the first 20 terms.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
$t_{20}=5\times1.2^{19}=159.7$ M1: Use of $t_n=ar^{n-1}$; A1: cao
$S_{20}=\frac{5(1-1.2^{20})}{1-1.2}=933.4$ M1: Use of a correct sum formula with n=19 or n=20. NB if n=19 is used and no formula is quoted, score M0; A1: cao

parts.label: b
parts.text:
The sum of the first $n$ terms of the series is greater than 3000
(b) Calculate the smallest possible value of $n$.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
$\frac{5(1-1.2^n)}{1-1.2}(>\text{ or }=)3000$ B1: Correct statement (allow 'a' and/or 'r' instead of 5 and 1.2)
$1.2^n>121$ M1: Correct statement (>or<or=) k
$\log1.2^n>\log121$ or $n>\log_{1.2}121$ M1: Takes logs correctly
$n>\frac{\log121}{\log1.2}$ i.e. $n=27$ A1: cao
Ignore symbols e.g. '=' throughout with no errors getting n=27 scores full marks
In (b) treat $5\times1.2^{n-1}>3000$ as a misread and allow the M's if scored (gives n=37)

questions.stem:
The height of water, $H$ metres, in a harbour on a particular day is given by the equation
$H=10+5\sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{6}\right)$, $0\leqslant t<24$
where $t$ is the number of hours after midnight.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Show that the height of the water 1 hour after midnight is 12.5 metres.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
$H=10+5\sin\left(\frac{\pi(1)}{6}\right)=12.5$* B1: 12.5 oe
Official notes (completeness pass):
- Or just $H=10+5\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=12.5$*

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Find, to the nearest minute, the times before midday when the height of the water is 9 metres.
(6)
parts.mark_scheme:
$9=10+5\sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{6}\right)\Rightarrow5\sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{6}\right)=-1$ M1: Proceed to $5\sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{6}\right)=k$. May be implied by e.g. $\sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{6}\right)=-\frac{1}{5}$
$\sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{6}\right)=-\frac{1}{5}\Rightarrow\left(\frac{\pi t}{6}\right)=\arcsin\left(\pm\frac{1}{5}\right)$ M1: $\arcsin\left(\pm\frac{k}{5}\right)$
$\alpha=\pm0.2(0135792)$ (or 11.536... degrees) B1: May be implied. Given the similarity between $-\frac{1}{5}$ and $\arcsin\left(-\frac{1}{5}\right)$ allow $\alpha=$awrt $\pm0.2$
$\left(\frac{\pi t}{6}\right)=\pi+0.201...$ or $\left(\frac{\pi t}{6}\right)=2\pi-0.201...$
$\left(\frac{\pi t}{6}\right)=3.34295...$ or $\left(\frac{\pi t}{6}\right)=6.08127...$
$=6.384565...$ or $11.615434...$ M1: May be implied. Do not allow mixing of degrees and radians but allow working in just degrees.
$t=$ 0623, 1137 A1,A1: Accept 6hrs 23mins, 11hrs 37mins Or 5hrs 37mins, 23 mins before midday

parts.text:
Given that
$\log_x(7y+1)-\log_x(2y)=1$, $x>4$, $0<y<1$
express $y$ in terms of $x$.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
$\log_x(7y+1)-\log_x2y=\log_x\left(\frac{7y+1}{2y}\right)$ B1: Combines logs correctly
$1=\log_x x$ B1: Correct statement (may be implied)
$\frac{7y+1}{2y}=x$ M1: Remove logs to obtain this equation or equivalent.
$2yx=7y+1\Rightarrow y(2x-7)=1$ dM1: Isolate y correctly to give y as a function of x. Allow sign errors only. Dependent on the previous method mark.
$y=\frac{1}{2x-7}$ or $\frac{-1}{7-2x}$ A1: cao
Way 2: $\log_x(7y+1)=1+\log_x2y$; $\log_x(7y+1)=\log_xx+\log_x2y$; $1=\log_xx$ (may be implied) B1; $\log_xx+\log_x2y=\log_x2xy$ B1: Combines logs correctly; $7y+1=2xy$ M1: Remove logs to obtain this equation or equivalent; then as above dM1, A1
Way 3: $\log_x(7y+1)-\log_x2y=\log_x\left(\frac{7y+1}{2y}\right)$ B1: Combines logs correctly; $\log_x\left(\frac{7y+1}{2y}\right)=\frac{\log_{10}\left(\frac{7y+1}{2y}\right)}{\log_{10}x}$ B1: Correct change of base; $\log_{10}\left(\frac{7y+1}{2y}\right)=\log_{10}x$; $\frac{7y+1}{2y}=x$ M1: Remove logs to obtain this equation or equivalent; Then as above

questions.stem:
Figure 1 shows a sketch of part of the curve $C$ with equation
$y=x^3-6x^2+9x+5$
The point $P(4,9)$ lies on $C$.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Show that the normal to $C$ at the point $P$ has equation
$x+9y=85$
(6)
parts.mark_scheme:
$\frac{dy}{dx}=3x^2-12x+9$ M1: $x^n\to x^{n-1}$; A1: Correct derivative
$\mathrm{f}'(4)=3(4)^2-12(4)+9=9$ M1: Finds f'(4)
$m_N=-\frac{1}{\text{"9"}}$ dM1: Perpendicular gradient rule applied to their f'(4). Dependent on the previous method mark.
$y-9=\text{"-}\frac{1}{9}\text{"}(x-4)$ ddM1: Correct straight line method as shown or y=mx+c with an attempt to find c. Depends on both previous method marks.
$x+9y=85$* A1*: Correct completion to printed answer. Allow this from the previous line.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
The region $R$, shown shaded in Figure 1, is bounded by the curve $C$, the $y$-axis and the normal to $C$ at $P$.
(b) Showing all your working, calculate the exact area of $R$.
(7)
parts.mark_scheme:
Way 1: $x=0\Rightarrow y=\frac{85}{9}$
Area trapezium=$\frac{1}{2}\times4\times\left(9+\frac{85}{9}\right)$ ($=\frac{332}{9}=36.88...$) M1: Correct method for trapezium; A1: Correct numerical expression
$\int y\,dx=\frac{x^4}{4}-2x^3+\frac{9x^2}{2}+5x$ M1: $x^n\to x^{n+1}$; A1: Correct integration
$\left[\frac{x^4}{4}-2x^3+\frac{9x^2}{2}+5x\right]_0^4=\frac{4^4}{4}-2\times4^3+\frac{9\times4^2}{2}+5\times4-(0)$ M1: Use of limits 0 and 4 in a changed function and subtracts (either way round) (-0 may be implied)
$R=\frac{332}{9}-28=\frac{80}{9}$ M1: Their Trapezium – Their Integral or Their Integral – Their Trapezium; A1: Cso
Way 2: Area trapezium=$\int_0^4\left(\frac{85-x}{9}\right)dx=\left[\frac{85x-\frac{x^2}{2}}{9}\right]$ M1: Correct method for trapezium including limits. An attempt to integrate their rearrangement of the normal with the limits 0 and 4.; $=\frac{1}{9}\left(85(4)-\frac{4^2}{2}\right)(-0)$ A1: Correct numerical expression; $\int y\,dx=\frac{x^4}{4}-2x^3+\frac{9x^2}{2}+5x$ M1A1: Correct integration; use of limits 0 and 4 (either way round, -0 may be implied) M1; $R=\frac{332}{9}-28=\frac{80}{9}$ M1A1: Trapezium-Integral or Integral-Trapezium, Cso
Way 3: Line-Curve=$\frac{85-x}{9}-(x^3-6x^2+9x+5)$ M1A1 (first 2 marks; allow Curve-Line for both marks; A1 not awarded if brackets missing unless correct expression implied by later work); $\int(y_1-y_2)dx=\frac{1}{9}\int(40-9x^3+54x^2-82x)dx$; $=\frac{1}{9}\left[40x-\frac{9x^4}{4}+\frac{54x^3}{3}-\frac{82x^2}{2}\right]$ M2A1: M2: $x^n\to x^{n+1}$ on both line and curve, second and third M's, second A: correct integration; use of limits 0 and 4 in a changed function and subtracts (either way round) M1; $\frac{1}{9}\left[40(4)-\frac{9(4)^4}{4}+\frac{54(4)^3}{3}-\frac{82(4)^2}{2}\right](-0)=\frac{80}{9}$ or any exact equivalent A1cso. If the only error in this method is to do (Curve-Line) then only penalise the final mark – i.e. they get -80/9
